claims.claim: Didymus the Blind (Didymus Caecus) was a Christian theologian and head of the Alexandrian catechetical school, born around 313 and died around 398 in Alexandria, Egypt.
He was blind from early childhood, remained a layman, and was a student of Origen who was known for opposing Arianism.
His Commentary on Ecclesiastes was written in the late fourth century as a lecturing exegesis intended for his students at the Alexandrian school.
The work was lost to the medieval West because Didymus’ writings were condemned at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553 for Origenist doctrines, leading to few manuscript copies.
The manuscript of the Commentary on Ecclesiastes survived in a papyrus codex (the Tura Codex) discovered in 1941 in a subterranean cavern at Tura, near Cairo, during World II.
After its discovery the papyrus was recovered, is now housed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, and has been edited by Otto Guéraud and published in the series Papyrologische Texte und Abhandlungen.
Photographs of the papyrus pages have been posted online, and the text is entered in the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae database.

The commentary is significant because it preserves Didymus’ exegetical method, includes citations of previously unknown Greek pagan authors, and provides a rare example of his biblical interpretation after most of his works were lost.
